objection: If Jesus is God, why did he pray to God?
answer:
Brother, the objection rightly takes the prayers seriously, and I won't minimize them. But notice what they actually reveal. Colossians 2:9 tells us that all the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily — Paul is not describing a divine visitor wearing a costume of flesh, but God truly and permanently incarnate. That means Jesus possesses a genuine human nature, with a human mind, will, and body, alongside his divine nature. It is that human nature which kneels in Gethsemane and cries out in dependence — not because deity itself lacks anything, but because the Son has actually become what he was not before: a man, who hungers, weeps, and prays as men do. This is not deception; it is the reality of the incarnation, which Philippians 2 describes as Christ, existing in the form of God, genuinely humbling himself and taking the form of a servant.

John 17:3 shows Jesus praying to "the only true God" while personally distinct from the Father — but distinction of persons is not denial of shared deity; the same Gospel opens with the Word being God and closes with Thomas confessing him as "my Lord and my God." The Son's prayer expresses the eternal order between Father and Son, not an ontological gap between God and a creature. And strikingly, the early church, having watched him pray, turned around and prayed to him: Stephen cries, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59), and believers are those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:2). They saw no contradiction between his praying as man and his being invoked as God — because both flow from one truth: the eternal Son, without ceasing to be God, truly became man to save man.

# The Prayer Objection

Brother, consider: Jesus prayed — not once or in passing, but throughout his ministry. In Gethsemane, he fell on his face and begged his Father, "If it be possible, let this cup pass from me" (Matthew 26:39). He prayed before choosing the apostles, before feeding the five thousand, at his baptism. A man who genuinely prays, who asks God for something he does not possess, who depends utterly on another's will — how can such a one *be* God? God does not beseech himself. God does not have needs. Yet Jesus demonstrates every mark of a servant in submission to the one he calls "my God and your God" (John 20:17). If he truly were God, would this not be deception — the performance of dependence, the feigning of weakness?

This is one of the strongest objections, and the answer lies not in denying that Jesus prayed, but in understanding *who* was praying and *why*.

Colossians 2:9 tells us that all the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily — that is, in his incarnate humanity. Philippians 2:5-11 tells us how: the one who existed in the form of God took the form of a servant, becoming genuinely human. Gethsemane is not the Son's divine nature groaning under compulsion; it is the true human nature of the incarnate Son, facing real dread of suffering and death, submitting his human will to the Father's. That submission is not play-acting — it is the real, costly obedience of the "form of a servant," and it is precisely this humbling that Philippians says the Father exalts and rewards with the Name above every name.

John 17:3 is instructive here too: Jesus prays to the Father as "the only true God," distinguishing himself personally from the Father, without that distinction excluding him from the divine identity. The Son can address the Father as "my God" because he is genuinely, fully human as well as fully God — two natures, one person. It's the same logic behind Hebrews' citation of Psalm 45:6, where the Father calls the Son "O God" even while the Son remains eternally distinct from the Father in person.

So prayer doesn't reveal Jesus is *less* than God; it reveals that the eternal Son *became* a man who has a human mind, will, and voice capable of asking, fearing, and submitting — while never ceasing to be, in his own person, the one who created and reconciles all things (Colossians 1:15-20), and the one the earliest Christians themselves called upon in prayer as Lord (Acts 7:59, 1 Corinthians 16:22). That the Church prayed *to* Jesus even while Jesus prayed *to* the Father is not contradiction but Trinity: one God in three Persons, the Son now also truly man, addressing the Father he has never ceased to be one with.

That means Jesus possesses a genuine human nature, with a human mind, will, and body, alongside his divine nature. It is that human nature which kneels in Gethsemane and cries out in dependence — not because deity itself lacks anything, but because the Son has actually become what he was not before: a man, who hungers, weeps, and prays as men do. This is not deception; it is the reality of the incarnation, which Philippians 2 describes as Christ, existing in the form of God, genuinely humbling himself and taking the form of a servant.

John 17:3 shows Jesus praying to "the only true God" while personally distinct from the Father — but distinction of persons is not denial of shared deity; the same Gospel opens with the Word being God and closes with Thomas confessing him as "my Lord and my God." The Son's prayer expresses the eternal order between Father and Son, not an ontological gap between God and a creature.
